**Owner review of the pull request.** The owner's adversarial review of the pull request (static, on its description and diff) withheld approval for six findings, all fixed in the pull request before merging:
1. *The wire helper took any send error for a reset.* `h1_until_close_or_reset` set its reset flag on every exception from `write_all` and then stopped reading, and `test_http1_receive_limit_counts_buffered_bytes` accepted a bare `<reset>`: a timeout or a request never sent could have passed as Flare's refusal. Now `_is_reset` accepts only Flare's `ConnectionReset` and `BrokenPipe`, the only errors measured after a refusal; any other error, a timeout included, raises, and the helper reads after a reset write too, since an answer may already have arrived (the keep-alive helper's follow-up write uses the same rule). The refusal is now shown without a race: `h1_buffered_threshold` sends an unfinished request of one-byte chunks with a limit of 4096 up to exactly 4096 + 8192 bytes, sees no answer for 1 s on an open connection, sends one byte more, and gets Flare's 413 (`Connection: close`, body `413 Content Too Large`) and a clean close, no reset or other error tolerated. Flare had read every byte sent, so it closes with a FIN; the body sent so far is about 2 KB, so the chunk scanner cannot be what refused; nothing reached the middleware. The two racing cases (the whole 24.7 KB, and 16 KiB of chunks with a limit of 64) stay as observations, with only those two errors tolerated.
2. *`FLARE_BUFRING_HANDLER=1` was untested.* Read in Flare's source: the buffer-ring reader appends what the kernel delivered with `_append_pre_recv_bytes`, which makes the same buffered-bytes comparison, and parses with the same `max_body_size` checks as the unified loop. Measured with `Server` (Linux 6.18, io_uring available) and the variable set in the serving child: with a limit of 64, over `Content-Length` and chunked, 0, 63 and 64 bytes arrived byte for byte, and 65 and 4096 bytes got the same refusals as on the unified loop on every route, with no middleware, conversion or handler run; a head declaring 65 was refused at once and the keep-alive connection closed. That loop closes an h2c connection, which tells it from the unified loop on the wire. But it does not answer a request longer than 8192 bytes on the wire (one buffer-ring buffer): 8192 bytes were answered and 8193 were not, with `Content-Length` or chunked, for bodies far within the limit (100 KB with the default 10 MiB) and for the buffered-bytes threshold, and while such a request was pending the server answered no other connection and used about 80% of a CPU, until Flare's 60 s request timeout answered the stuck request 408 (after 48 to 57 s); with a limit of 4096 the server then answered a new connection (once, with 10 MiB, the next connection was reset instead; not investigated further). The same 8192/8193 boundary reproduces with Flare v0.12.0 alone (`HttpServer` with its default configuration and a plain handler, no Muntin), so it is a Flare defect, independent of `max_body_bytes`. Decision: Muntin does not support serving with the variable set, and says so in `docs/DX.md` section 1, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and the adapter's docstring; `test_receive_limit_on_flare_bufring_path` records the answers within 8192 bytes and pins the defect (8192 answered; 8193, and a `GET` on another connection meanwhile, unanswered for 1 s), so a Flare release that fixes it turns the test red. It skips on macOS, where Flare reads the variable on Linux only, and on a Linux host without io_uring unless `CI` is set, where it fails. Not chosen in this round: making `Server.serve` raise when the variable is set (a run-time behaviour change for a program that sets it today, left to the owner, who chose it in the re-review below), clearing the variable in `serve` (it would change the process's environment), and working around the defect in the adapter (a Flare cause; Muntin core is not changed for it). `Upgrade: h2c` remains read in Flare's source only, as before.
3. *"The largest request body Flare receives" overstated the contract.* The measured 413 for a within-limit body in one-byte chunks shows `max_body_bytes` bounds what is received but does not promise to accept every body within it. The adapter's docstrings, `docs/DX.md` section 1 (the lead and the example's sentence), `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/SPEC.md`, `README.md` and this record's selection now say "upper bound", and name what can refuse a body within it; an invariant above keeps it so.
4. *The h2c test client never acknowledged the server's SETTINGS* (RFC 9113 section 6.5.3). `h2_upload` now sends `SETTINGS` with `ACK` for each non-ACK `SETTINGS` it reads; every h2c case passes with it. Flare v0.12.0 tolerated the missing acknowledgement, so no test turns red without it. The older `_h2_answers` helper (from M3-039, used by earlier cases) does not acknowledge either; it is left as it is, outside this item.
5. *`RST_STREAM` error codes were read with the top bit masked.* `_be32` dropped bit 31, which is reserved only in `WINDOW_UPDATE`, so a code such as 0x8000000B would have read as 11. Now `_u32` keeps every bit (`RST_STREAM`), and `_window_increment` masks bit 31 (`WINDOW_UPDATE`); `test_h2_client_decodes_rst_stream_codes_with_every_bit` checks both.
6. *The M3-032 record said "None is exposed" and named M3-044 in one sentence.* It is restored to the state when M3-032 was decided, with a note that M3-044 later added the argument.

Mutations for the new tests, on scratch copies, run with the three new or changed tests: the HTTP/1.1 field left at Flare's default turns `test_http1_receive_limit_counts_buffered_bytes` and `test_receive_limit_on_flare_bufring_path` red; the value +1 turns both red (the threshold test sees no answer at one byte more); the value −1 turns both red; masking bit 31 in `_u32` turns `test_h2_client_decodes_rst_stream_codes_with_every_bit` red. Removing the `SETTINGS` acknowledgement, or widening `_is_reset` to every error, turns nothing red: Flare tolerates the first, and no test produces another error for the second; those are test-client correctness, not evidence.

A fresh-context review scoped to these fixes found one over-promise, now corrected: `docs/DX.md` said a `Content-Length` request with a head under 8 KiB and nothing pipelined after it is always received within the limit, but Flare drains a whole burst before parsing, so a request pipelined before it counts too (reproduced: with a limit of 64, a 64-byte body sent alone was answered 200, and the same request sent right after a body-less `GET` with an 8,141-byte head, in one 8,278-byte burst, was 413 and never received). It also corrected a docstring's byte range and the 408's timing (Flare's request timeout, 60 s by default, answered after 48 to 57 s when measured), and replaced restated buffer-ring details in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `AGENT_PROGRESS.md` and the adapter's docstring with a pointer to `docs/DX.md` section 1. Noted, not changed: on macOS a `send` racing a peer's teardown can fail with `EPROTOTYPE`, which Flare reports as `NetworkError` and `_is_reset` does not accept; it has not occurred, and if a racing case flakes that way it is an OS cause, not Muntin's.

**Owner re-review.** The owner approved the API, the 2^59 − 1 range and the six fixes, and asked for two changes, both made:
1. *Fail fast instead of only documenting the buffer-ring loop as unsupported.* The variable comes from outside the application, the defect stalls the whole server, and Muntin is pre-release, so `Server.serve` now raises `FLARE_BUFRING_HANDLER=1 is unsupported by Muntin with Flare v0.12.0` before calling Flare's `serve` when `getenv("FLARE_BUFRING_HANDLER") == "1"`, the comparison Flare's `_resolve_bufring_handler_env` makes. The check runs on every system, not only where Flare would take that loop (Linux with io_uring): the same environment then starts or fails alike on a developer's macOS and a Linux host, and the refusal is tested on both CI systems. The price is that a host where the variable did nothing (macOS, Linux without io_uring) now refuses it too; the remedy is to unset it. `ServerConfig.use_bufring`, the loop's other switch, stays at Flare's default (`False`): `_server_config` never sets it. Red before the guard: `test_serve_refuses_flare_bufring_handler` (in `adapters/flare/test_server.mojo`, the variable set only in a forked child) saw the child killed by its 10-second alarm (signal 14) inside Flare's loop instead of exiting with the refusal; with the guard it exits with the refusal, and with `0` it serves. Mutations: the guard removed turns that test red (the alarm), and a guard that refuses any value turns it red (the `0` case). The pin moved off `Server`: `test_receive_limit_on_flare_bufring_path` now serves through Flare's own `HttpServer` with `_server_config(limit)` and `MuntinHandler` (`_serve_flare_bufring_in_child`), so it keeps watching Flare's loop with Muntin's configuration and handler.

The test now opens that connection, sends the 8,193 bytes, sees the read time out, sends `GET /hello` on a second connection and sees that time out too, and only then closes both, explicitly, so the first stays open for the whole check. This matches the stated condition; it does not change what the test can detect. The scoped review of this change closed the first connection before the `GET` and the server still answered nothing, because it keeps spinning on the request it already received, so the old test did observe a stall, and losing the hold turns no test red.

### Graceful shutdown decision (M3-045)

Status: **decision and production** (M3-045, [pull request #83](https://github.com/sano-suguru/muntin/pull/83)). It decides how a `Server` stops when the process is asked to stop (SIGTERM from a supervisor on deploy or restart, SIGINT from Ctrl-C), which [M3-032](#serving-entrypoint-decision-m3-032) left out ("Muntin adds no stop call, graceful shutdown or signal handling") with a revisit condition ("Flare offers a stop the serving thread can request, or the toolchain gives the process a thread or signal primitive Muntin would use"), and implements the choice in the same item. The question, candidates, criteria and pass conditions below were written before the wire measurements; what precedes them was read from Muntin's and Flare v0.12.0's source and from three probes of Mojo 1.1.0 (named below).

**Why now.** Every deploy or restart of a `Server` program cuts the requests it is answering: SIGTERM ends the process by the runtime's re-raise (M3-032, measured), with nothing drained. That is the largest remaining obstacle to running a `Server` behind a supervisor.

**Question.** When a serving process receives SIGTERM (and SIGINT, if the same policy fits), can `Server.serve` (1) stop accepting new connections, (2) let the requests already in progress finish and reach their clients, and (3) end within a bounded time whatever clients and handlers do; and with what API (does `server.serve(app)` keep its spelling, is there a stop handle, where the time bound is set, its default and range), what serve returns or how the process exits, and what is promised about new connections, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, h2c connections, partly received bodies and handlers that do not return.

**The path at the base** (read from the code and probed):
- Flare v0.12.0's single-worker `serve` runs `run_unified_reactor_loop` on the calling thread. The loop re-reads `HttpServer._stopping` (an acquire load through its address) once per iteration; its poll waits at most 100 ms, and `epoll_wait`/`kevent` interrupted by a signal (EINTR) count as an empty poll. A handler runs synchronously inside the loop, so the flag is not read while one runs; an HTTP/1.1 response is written eagerly right after the handler returns. When the loop sees the flag it flips `Cancel.SHUTDOWN` on every live connection (h2c: `signal_drain`, which sends nothing) and closes each, then `serve` returns.
- `HttpServer.close()` sets the flag and closes the listener ("hard stop"). `HttpServer.drain(timeout_ms)` closes the listener, sleeps the whole `timeout_ms` while the reactor keeps serving the open connections, then sets the flag; its documentation and Flare's operations guide say it is called "from a thread other than the one running serve()", that it cannot return early (the single-worker reactor publishes no live-connection count), and that Flare installs no signal handler because "Mojo does not yet allow the process-global mutable state an async-signal-safe handler needs". `ServerConfig.shutdown_timeout_ms` (default 5000) is a stored value `drain` does not read. Flare's own background-thread pattern is `flare.runtime.watchdog` (a control block and `ThreadHandle.spawn_os`).
- Probes (Mojo 1.1.0, Linux x86-64): a module-level `var` does not compile (`global variables are not supported`); a Mojo binary has five threads before `main` does anything (the runtime's four `🔥 Thread` workers), none of them blocking any signal, and the runtime has a handler on SIGINT and SIGTERM in every thread's process (`SigCgt`), installed over an inherited `SIG_IGN` too (a process started with both ignored showed them caught, not ignored); a `sigaction` with `SA_RESETHAND` and a handler that does nothing let the process survive SIGTERM, and a later `sigaction` read showed the disposition reset to `SIG_DFL`.

**Candidates.**
- A, a Muntin stop mechanism: the adapter turns SIGTERM/SIGINT into a stop request without a global and without work in the signal handler, and a helper thread carries the request to Flare (close the listener, keep serving for a bounded window, then stop).
- B, wrap Flare's lifecycle API minimally: as A, but the helper thread calls Flare's own `drain(timeout_ms)` and Muntin adds only the signal detection, the bound on the whole stop and the restore.
- B0, signal handler sets Flare's stop flag directly, no thread: the handler writes `_stopping`.
- C, decision only: if no candidate both finishes in-flight requests and bounds the stop, record what Flare would need and change nothing.

**Comparison criteria**: whether in-flight requests finish and reach the client; whether new connections are refused; whether the stop is bounded when a client stalls or a handler never returns; what runs in the signal handler (nothing that allocates, raises, locks or touches a Flare or Mojo object); global state needed; threads added and their lifetime; the API added and whether `server.serve(app)` keeps building; HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and h2c behavior during the window, measured; exit status; Linux and macOS.

**Pass conditions** (each with executable evidence on the wire, a real child process, on both CI systems):
- an HTTP/1.1 request whose handler is waiting when SIGTERM arrives is released after the signal and its response (status and body that only the released handler can produce) reaches the client; the child then ends with the documented status, within the documented bound;
- after SIGTERM, a new connection is refused within the documented time; what an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection and an h2c connection open before the signal see during the window and at its end is measured and only what holds is promised;
- with no request at all, SIGTERM ends the child within the bound; with a client that sent half a request and stalls, and with a handler that never returns, the child still ends within the bound, with the status the record names for each;
- the parent reaps every child it forks, kills it if it outlives the bound (the test then fails, not hangs), and the port can be bound again after the child ends;
- SIGINT: the in-flight case and the no-request case as for SIGTERM; a second stop signal during the window and the bound value's range checked;
- existing `Server` tests, the loopback suite (HTTP/1.1 and h2c, raw and typed handlers), M3-044's receive limit and refusal, `_BorrowedHandler`'s non-`Copyable` guard and the serving fixtures keep passing;
- scratch mutations turning a listed test red: the signal ignored (no stop request), the drain skipped (stop at once), the bound removed;
- `src/muntin` unchanged; `check_boundaries.sh` passes.

**Measured premises** (Mojo 1.1.0, Flare v0.12.0, Linux x86-64; the final tests in `adapters/flare/test_server.mojo`, run first against a scratch copy of the adapter, then against the code):
- **Notification.** A handler that does nothing, installed with `SA_RESETHAND | SA_RESTART`, lets the process survive SIGTERM and SIGINT on whichever thread receives them, and the disposition reads `SIG_DFL` afterwards; a thread polling `sigaction` every 50 ms saw it within that time. Nothing else is needed in signal context, and no global.
- **Flare's `drain` from a second thread** (a pthread through Flare's `ThreadHandle.spawn_os`, given the `HttpServer`'s address while the serving thread is inside Flare's `serve`): new connections were refused 48 to 53 ms after the signal; an HTTP/1.1 request whose handler was blocked when SIGTERM (or SIGINT) arrived, released after the refusal was seen, was answered 200 with the body only the released handler produces, and the child exited 0 about 1,610 ms after the signal with a 1,500 ms window; with 300 ms and no request it exited after about 425 ms, with 0 after about 125 ms. A connection opened while the handler blocked the reactor (queued by the system, not yet accepted by Flare) was reset with no answer when the listener closed.
- **During the window:** an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection that had been answered before SIGTERM got a second request answered after the refusal (`200`, `Connection: keep-alive`), then was closed 500 ms later (Flare's `idle_timeout_ms`); on an h2c connection whose stream 1 was blocked in its handler, stream 3, sent after the refusal, was answered too, both after the release, and the connection was closed about 550 ms after the signal, before the window ended, with no `GOAWAY`.
- **Bounds:** a client that sent a head declaring 100 bytes and 10 of them did not delay the stop (exit 0 after the window) and got no answer. A handler that never returned held the reactor past the window: Flare's `serve` did not return, and only the watcher's `_exit(128 + 15)` ended the child, 1,350 ms after the signal with a 300 ms window and a 1 s bound. A second SIGTERM or SIGINT after the refusal ended the child by that signal within 5 ms.
- **Mojo:** a `sigaction` buffer must stay alive past the call (a `List` destroyed after its last named use was read freed: the first prototype installed a garbage handler and crashed); one module-wide signature per C symbol (`write`, `_exit` conflict with the standard library's and Flare's declarations).

**Candidates, compared.**

| Candidate | In-flight requests | New connections | Bounded | Signal context | Threads | API | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: Muntin's own drain (close the listener, its own wait, set Flare's flag) | finish (as B) | refused | yes | nothing | one watcher | as B | rejected: it would reimplement `drain` against Flare's private fields (`_listener`, `_stopping`) for no difference on the wire; an early return, its one possible gain, needs a live count Flare does not publish |
| B: Flare's `drain` called by a watcher thread; the signal seen through `SA_RESETHAND` | finish within the window (tested, HTTP/1.1 and h2c) | refused within about 50 ms (Linux), 170 to 185 ms (macOS CI) | yes: the window plus 1 s, then `_exit(128 + signal)` | nothing | one watcher, joined before `serve` returns | `shutdown_grace_ms` on `bind`; `serve(app)` unchanged | **chosen** |
| B0: the signal handler writes Flare's stop flag | a running handler finishes and its eager HTTP/1.1 write goes out, but a request still arriving, a pending write and every other h2c stream are cut | open until the reactor exits | only between events | writes a Flare object's field, through an address the handler cannot find without a global | none | as B | rejected: it is `close()`, Flare's hard stop, not graceful; and Mojo 1.1.0 has no global for the address |
| B1: mask the signals and `sigwait` in the watcher, no handler | as B | as B | as B | nothing | one | as B | rejected: the runtime's four worker threads do not block the signals, so the kernel delivers them there and the runtime's handler ends the process (measured threads and masks) |
| C: decision only | none | none | none | none | none | none | rejected: B meets the pass conditions |

**Selected: B.** `Server.bind(host, port, *, max_body_bytes=..., shutdown_grace_ms: Int = 5000)`; `server.serve(app)` keeps its spelling and, while it runs, turns SIGTERM and SIGINT into a graceful stop: the listener closes, the open connections are served for the whole window, Flare closes the rest and `serve` returns normally. Contract: `docs/DX.md` section 1; mechanism: `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Flare adapter".
- **Why a thread.** Flare's reactor gives Muntin control only inside a handler and reads only its own stop flag; `drain` is documented as called from another thread. One watcher thread is the least that reaches it: it starts and is joined inside `serve`, touches no `App`, and uses Flare's own thread handle (an internal module, `flare.runtime._thread`, the one Flare's watchdog uses), so Muntin adds no thread code of its own.
- **Why `SA_RESETHAND`.** Mojo 1.1.0 has no module-level state, so a handler cannot tell anyone anything by writing memory; a blocked-signal design fails on the runtime's threads (B1). The kernel's own reset of the disposition is state the watcher can read without any shared memory, and the handler is empty.
- **The window is waited in full.** Flare v0.12.0's single-worker reactor publishes no live-connection count, so neither `drain` nor Muntin can tell when the last request ended; returning when Muntin's own handler count reaches zero would cut a body still arriving or a response still being written. A stop with nothing in flight therefore takes the window.
- **The default, 5,000 ms,** is Flare's `ServerConfig.shutdown_timeout_ms` default: with the 1 s bound a stop ends within about 6 s, inside Docker's default 10 s and Kubernetes' default 30 s before they kill. **The range,** 0 to 86,400,000 (one day), keeps Flare's `now + timeout` and the watcher's deadline far from overflow and rejects what is almost certainly a unit mistake; it is checked by `bind` after `max_body_bytes` and before the host.
- **The bound, 1 s after the window,** is ten of the reactor's longest poll waits (100 ms): past it, only a running handler can be keeping the reactor, and Mojo cannot interrupt it. Exit status 128 + the signal is the shell's convention for "ended by that signal" and tells it apart from a stop that drained (0); `_exit` works for process 1 in a container, where the kernel ignores a re-raised default-action signal.
- **A second stop signal** takes the default action, so an operator can still force a stop (Ctrl-C twice).
- **Kept as before:** the receive limit and its refusals (M3-044), the buffer-ring refusal, HTTP/1.1 and h2c answers, raw and typed handlers, `_BorrowedHandler`'s non-`Copyable` guard (the watcher never touches the handler), `App.handle` on one thread, `src/muntin`.

**By kind (M2-016): not an M2 reopen.** `App.handle`, the accepted set, the overload set and every diagnostic are unchanged; `Server` is an M3 type. What changes is the adapter's runtime: during `serve`, SIGTERM and SIGINT no longer end the process at once (by the runtime's re-raise) but stop it gracefully, so a `main` that does nothing after `serve` now exits 0 after a stop instead of being terminated by the signal; a process that inherited them ignored now stops on them while it serves (the runtime already replaced that ignore before `main`). `Server.bind` gains one keyword-only argument with a default.

**Cost.** One more thread for the life of `serve`, polling every 50 ms. Every stop takes the whole window. The handlers of SIGTERM and SIGINT belong to `serve` while it runs. Muntin depends on an internal Flare module (`flare.runtime._thread`) and on `struct sigaction`'s layout and flag values on Linux (glibc) and macOS, written in the adapter. No GOAWAY or `Connection: close` during the window: keep-alive clients learn of the stop by a closed connection.

**What Flare would need for more** (upstream, not required by this item): the single-worker reactor publishing its live-connection count (as its multi-worker workers do through their stats cell) would let `drain` return when the last connection closes; sending GOAWAY and `Connection: close` while draining would tell keep-alive clients before the close; a public thread handle or a stop request the serving thread can make would remove the internal import.

**Revisit when:** Flare publishes a live-connection count, a public thread handle or a serving-thread stop; Flare's `drain` changes (returns early, sends GOAWAY or `Connection: close`, stops serving open connections), which the stop tests would show; the Mojo runtime changes its signal handlers or threads; Mojo gains module-level state (a handler could then write a flag, and the poll could go); applications need a stop call, an early return or a hook before the stop.

**Verification.** Red before the code: the stop tests did not build (no `shutdown_grace_ms`); with the keyword removed, every one of them failed on the base, the children ended by the runtime's handler. Scratch mutations: the handler not installed turned nine stop tests red; `close()` instead of `drain` turned six red (the window not waited, the in-flight and h2c cases); the `_exit` removed turned the never-returning handler's test red (the child outlived its bound and was killed by the test); the dispositions not put back turned every test that reaches the end of `serve` red (exit 4).

**Fresh-context review.** A review of the diff against Flare's source found no high-severity defect (the `struct sigaction` layouts and flags, the empty handler, the buffers' lifetimes and the spawn-failure restore checked out) and these, each acted on:
1. *The stop tests ran only in forked children,* which have neither the runtime's worker threads nor a `main` that returns, although ARCHITECTURE named an exec-based test as due once Muntin took on graceful shutdown. `adapters/flare/stop_driver.mojo`, built by `check_flare.sh`, is now `execv`d by two tests: a request held when SIGTERM arrives is answered and the program exits 0 by returning from `main` (six threads when counted by hand in `/proc`: the runtime's four, the main one and the watcher); started with SIGINT ignored, it still stops on SIGINT.
2. *A stop before Flare's `serve` set up its reactor* would make that `serve` raise on the closed listener (`drain` closes it before setting the flag), so `Server.serve` would raise on a stop. The watcher now records the signal it acts on, and `serve` returns normally when Flare's `serve` raised after one. Not pinned: the window is between `_StopWatch` and Flare's first poll, and no test can place a signal there.
3. *A second signal as process 1 of a container* takes the default action, which the kernel ignores there; `docs/DX.md` now says so and names `--init`.
4. *"The dispositions are back when it raises" had no evidence.* Each stop test's child now serves a second time on the closed listener, which raises, and checks the dispositions again; skipping the restore on that path turned nine tests red.
5. *A stop signal arriving as `serve` ends for another reason* was swallowed by the empty handler. `finish` now sends it again once the previous dispositions are back. A SIGINT within the watcher's 50 ms poll after a SIGTERM is absorbed rather than ending the process; `docs/DX.md` says the second signal counts once the stop has begun. Neither timing can be placed by a test.
6. *Two lower bounds were measured from the start of the reap,* not from the signal; they now use a timestamp taken before `kill`.
7. *Forked children inherited the runner's ignored SIGPIPE;* each now restores the default right after `fork`.
8. *"Reset" was stronger than its test* (which also accepted EOF); `docs/DX.md` says closed without an answer, reset when measured on Linux.
9. *Code that resets a stop signal to the default during `serve` starts a stop;* `docs/DX.md` says so.

A review scoped to those fixes found no high-severity defect and these, each acted on: the module docstring, `serve`'s docstring, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and `docs/DX.md` still said a raise always propagates (now they state the exception, and that a Flare setup failure coinciding with a stop is dropped with it); a signal could still slip between `finish`'s check and the restore (the restore now reads each disposition it replaces in the same `sigaction` call); the exec'd driver had no `alarm` (a driver stalling before its port would hang the run) and the helper leaked a pipe and the child on a failed read (both fixed); the ignored-SIGINT test's docstring credited the runtime for what `serve`'s unconditional handler does (reworded); the thread count was not measured by a test (marked as counted by hand). It confirmed that a second `serve` on the closed listener raises (`fcntl` on fd -1) on Linux and macOS without creating a reactor, and that a signal is never sent again after a stop the watcher drained.

**macOS** (the CI runner, arm64; first run of the stop tests there): all 28 `Server` tests passed, `::1` included. New connections were refused 167 to 185 ms after the signal (50 ms on Linux); an in-flight request was answered and the child exited 0 about 1,950 ms after the signal with a 1,500 ms window; the never-returning handler ended with 143 after 1,453 ms (300 ms window); keep-alive and h2c behaved as on Linux (no `GOAWAY`), and a queued connection was reset. The first macOS run did not build the tests: Flare's macOS reactor declares `pipe` with a pointer argument, which conflicted with the test helper's own declaration; the helper now uses Flare's wrapper.

**Owner review of the pull request.** The owner's adversarial review (static, of the adapter and test diff) confirmed the main path (the `SA_RESETHAND` notification, Flare's `drain`, the `_exit` bound, which works for process 1) and withdrew an earlier remark about process 1; it accepted the 5 s default and the window waited in full. It withheld approval for one blocking finding and five more, each acted on:
1. *Two `serve`s in one process corrupted the process-wide dispositions* (blocking). Each `_StopWatch` saved what it replaced, so a second one saved the first one's handler and, finishing last, put that handler back with no watcher behind it; finishing first, it could undo a stop the other still needed. Neither was refused nor documented. Decision: one `serve` per process owns the stop signals. `_StopWatch` first claims a process-wide cell (compare-and-swap from 0 to 1) and raises `Server.serve is already serving in this process` before touching any disposition when another holds it; it releases the cell after the restore, on every path. Mojo 1.1.0 has no module-level `var`, so the cell is created by the standard library's internal `std.ffi._get_global`, which creates a named global once per process under its own lock (probed: 16 threads racing to claim it, one won, three runs). Rejected: a process-level signal manager shared by several `serve`s (more machinery for a configuration nothing needs: a `Server` is one thread, and a process that needs several sockets can serve them from several processes); using the disposition itself as the lock (a second `serve` starting while the first is draining, with both dispositions back at `SIG_DFL`, would look free). Red on the base: `test_a_second_serve_in_the_process_is_refused`, where a handler of a serving `Server` binds and serves a second one, timed out (the second `serve` started its own watcher and Flare loop inside the handler). Mutations: the claim check removed turns that test red; the release skipped turns 14 tests red (`_serve_stoppable`'s second `serve` is then refused as already serving, exit 7). A forked child of a serving process inherits the claim, so a `serve` there is refused; nothing in Muntin forks.
2. *`sigaction` results were ignored.* A failed read in the watcher would have left the zeroed buffer looking like `SIG_DFL` and started a stop; a failed install would have served with one signal handled and the other not. Now an install that fails puts back what was changed (sending again a signal delivered meanwhile), releases the claim and raises before serving; a failed read is not a delivery (the watcher reads again); a failed restore makes `serve` raise. `ThreadHandle.join` raises only if `pthread_join` fails (Flare's contract; with a thread `spawn_os` created joinable and never detached, the possible errors do not apply); if it ever did, the watcher could still read the control block, so `finish` puts the dispositions back and aborts the process rather than free the block, instead of skipping the restore. None of these failures can be produced by a test on a supported system; they were checked by reading the code and are untested.
3. *The stop boundaries were declared untestable.* `serve` now takes a private `_stage` hook (not API, like the initializer's `_`-keywords), called with both handlers installed and the watcher not yet started, with the watcher running before Flare's `serve`, after Flare's `serve` ended while the watcher still runs, and after the join before the restore. Four tests place a SIGTERM at each point in a forked child that serves the same `Server` twice (the second time Flare's `serve` raises on the closed listener at once): at the first two points `serve` returns, with the dispositions back and the claim released (the second `serve` raises on the listener, not as already serving); after Flare's `serve` ended, the signal is either acted on or sent again (both outcomes accepted; the second was the one measured); after the join it is sent again and ends the process by SIGTERM (the runtime's handler being back). Each child's dispositions are compared before and after, and every child ends within its bound. Mutations: `serve` re-raising after a stop turns the four red; the resend removed turns the last two red. These show the watcher ends and the dispositions return at each boundary; that the watcher never touches the server after `serve` returns rests on the structure (it is joined in `finish`, before `serve` returns, and reads the server only after it saw a signal), not on a memory checker.
4. *A `drain` that raised fell back to `close` silently.* The watcher now keeps the error, still falls back to `close` (Flare's hard stop), and `serve`, after the join and the restore, raises `serve: the graceful stop failed and open connections were closed at once: Flare's drain raised: <error>` instead of returning as for a graceful stop. On Flare v0.12.0 `drain` cannot raise (its one fallible step, closing the listener, does not raise), so this path is untested. The bound is now stated as measured from `drain`'s return: the signal's detection (up to 50 ms), the window, then `_REACTOR_STOP_MS`.
5. *The h2c stop test did not acknowledge the server's SETTINGS,* the defect M3-044 fixed in another client, *and did not check how the connection ended.* It now sends SETTINGS with ACK for the server's SETTINGS, and asserts that the connection ended by a close or a reset (not the read timing out) within the window plus the bound (measured: closed after about 553 ms, three runs).
6. *The `struct sigaction` layout was split only by macOS or not.* The offsets and flags were verified on Linux x86-64 (glibc) and macOS arm64, the project's two platforms (`pixi.toml`), so `_StopWatch` now has a `comptime assert` admitting only those: cross-compiled, `hello_server` builds for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` and `arm64-apple-darwin` and fails the assertion for `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` and `x86_64-apple-darwin` (`CompilationTarget.is_apple_silicon()` failed for a cross-compiled arm64 target, so the macOS test is "not x86").

**Revisit when** (added): Mojo removes or changes `std.ffi._get_global` or gains module-level state (the serving cell moves to it); an application needs several `serve`s in one process (a shared signal manager); a new platform is supported (its layout and flags, then the assertion).

A fresh-context review scoped to these fixes found nothing blocking; its findings, each acted on:
- *A failed restore released the claim* although that signal might keep the stop handler with no watcher behind it, so a later `serve` would have saved that handler as the disposition to put back (the blocking finding, degraded). The claim now stays held when a restore fails (the install-failure and spawn-failure paths too), and `serve` raises saying the process cannot serve again; a signal delivered on the disposition that was put back is still sent again. `errno` is now taken at the failing call, not after later calls; the serving cell's allocation is checked (the process aborts without it); a raise from the cleanup after Flare's `serve` raised now carries Flare's error.
- *`test_a_stop_before_flare_serves_returns` relied on a 300 ms sleep* for the watcher to close the listener first; a late watcher would have let the test pass through the reactor instead. Its hook now waits until SIGINT reads `SIG_DFL` (the watcher resets it right before `drain`, whose first step closes the listener) and then 50 ms. `drain` then holds the watcher for the whole window, which is why Flare's `serve` meets a closed listener and raises.
- *The h2c test acknowledged the server's SETTINGS only after the stop.* Acknowledging them before the stop showed that Flare writes nothing on that connection while stream 1's handler holds the reactor (the read timed out), so the test now sends the preface and SETTINGS, reads the server's SETTINGS, acknowledges them, and only then opens stream 1. The connection's close at about 553 ms after the signal is Flare's 500 ms idle close (`docs/DX.md` section 1), not the end of the window.
- Not tested: a second `serve` from another thread (the same compare-and-swap as from inside a handler, which is tested; the claim itself was probed with 16 racing threads).

**Owner re-review of the pull request.** The owner accepted `_get_global` as a known internal-API risk and asked for three changes before approving, each made:
1. *The claim was released before a late signal was sent again.* Between the release and the `kill`, another thread's `serve` could claim and install its handler, so the resent signal would stop that `serve` instead (or be absorbed by it). `finish` now restores, sends the signal again, and only then releases the claim (when the restore succeeded; a failed restore still keeps it, and the restore failure, then a `drain` failure, are still raised after it). The install-failure and spawn-failure paths follow the same order. A fifth `_stage` point, `_STAGE_RESTORED`, comes after the restore and any resend and before the release. `test_a_stop_sent_again_is_sent_before_the_claim_is_released` gives SIGTERM a do-nothing handler with `SA_RESETHAND` before serving, so the resend is seen (that disposition goes back to `SIG_DFL`) without ending the child, places a SIGTERM after the join, and at `_STAGE_RESTORED` requires the claim still held and the resend delivered; after `serve` raises it requires the claim released. Mutations: releasing before the resend turns it red (exit 30, the claim already released); the resend removed turns it and both late-signal stage tests (after Flare's `serve`, after the join) red. A forked child has one thread, so the test cannot tell `raise` from `kill` to the process. The test's first form gave SIGTERM a do-nothing handler with `SA_RESETHAND` and failed on macOS CI only (exit 32, the resend never seen): macOS's `sigaction` does not report `SA_RESETHAND` in the disposition it returns (xnu's `sigaction` builds the old action's flags from `SA_ONSTACK`, `SA_RESTART`, `SA_SIGINFO` and `SA_NODEFER` only), so the handler `serve` put back had lost the flag. The test's handler now sets its signal back to `SIG_DFL` itself; `docs/DX.md` states the macOS loss for an application's own handler. The scoped review of this fix found the order alone insufficient: `kill(2)` to the process makes the signal pending before it returns, but with the runtime's worker threads not blocking signals the kernel may run a handler on another thread, after the release. The resend is now `raise(3)`, which sends it to the serving thread and returns only after its disposition was acted on (a terminating default ends the process, a handler has run, an ignored signal is dropped); a signal that thread blocks would stay pending on it, and Muntin blocks none.
2. *The watcher's two resets to `SIG_DFL` were unchecked.* If one failed, a stop signal could keep the stop handler and a second signal would be absorbed instead of ending the process. Decision: if either reset fails, the watcher ends the process at once with `_exit(128 + signal)`, the status of the existing bound, without draining. Continuing the graceful stop and raising afterwards was rejected: it keeps a stop that the documented second-signal escape no longer covers, for a 24-hour window at most, and adds state for a failure `sigaction` cannot produce here (only `EINVAL` or `EFAULT`, neither possible with these signals and buffers). Untested for that reason.
3. *Docs:* `docs/DX.md`'s Protocols line still said `max_body_bytes` was the only backend configuration (now with `shutdown_grace_ms`), and the adapter's docstring did not list `_shutdown_grace_ms` among the initializer's keywords.

**Owner's third review of the pull request.** The owner accepted the three changes above and leaned to approving, with one precondition to state before merging: `raise` acts on the signal before it returns only if the calling thread does not block it. A serving thread that blocks SIGTERM, while the runtime's threads do not, lets a late SIGTERM run the stop handler on another thread; `finish` restores, `raise` leaves the resend pending on the serving thread, the claim is released, a later `serve` installs its handler, and when the first thread unblocks SIGTERM that later `serve` stops. Decision: the supported contract excludes it. `serve` is supported only on a thread that blocks neither SIGTERM nor SIGINT, before or during the call; `docs/DX.md` section 1, `serve`'s docstring and `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` say so (Muntin blocks neither). Rejected: unblocking the signal around the resend (`pthread_sigmask`), which would deliver a signal the application chose to hold for its own `sigwait` or `signalfd`, and any mechanism keeping a pending resend from reaching the next `serve`, which is more machinery for a configuration Muntin does not create. Untested: a documented exclusion, not a path the code handles.

### Head-of-line blocking decision (M3-046)

Status: **decision** (M3-046, [pull request #84](https://github.com/sano-suguru/muntin/pull/84); `src/muntin` unchanged). [M3-032](#serving-entrypoint-decision-m3-032) chose one reactor thread for `Server.serve` and left a revisit condition: "an application needs more than one serving thread: revisit whether `App.handle` may run concurrently ([M3-001](#application-state-decision-m3-001) interior mutability, [M3-008](#json-codec-decision-m3-008) the JSON cap) and whether `Server` takes a worker count". This record measures what the one thread costs on the wire, and decides whether Muntin can change it now. The question, candidates, criteria and pass conditions below were written before the wire measurements.

**Why now.** `Server.serve` calls `App.handle` synchronously on Flare's one reactor thread, so one slow handler may hold every other request in the process. That is the largest remaining property of `Server` that applications cannot see from its API, and M3-045's stop tests already observed one symptom (a connection queued while a handler held the reactor was not accepted).

**Question.**
1. Over HTTP/1.1, while a handler on connection A has not returned, is a light `GET` on another connection B answered, or even accepted?
2. Over prior-knowledge h2c, while stream 1's handler has not returned, is stream 3 on the same connection answered? And a stream on another h2c connection?
3. Is the cause Muntin's code, Flare's single reactor, or the handler being synchronous: does Flare's own `HttpServer` with a Flare handler (no Muntin) behave the same?
4. With more workers, what improves: progress across connections, progress of streams within one h2c connection, or both? The two are not to be conflated.
5. Can any of it be had while `App.handle`, middleware, `State`, the borrowed `App` and `_BorrowedHandler`'s non-`Copyable` guard keep their contracts, with the ownership, data races and lifetimes explained rather than asserted?

**What settles it:**
- the serving path in Muntin's adapter and Flare v0.12.0's single- and multi-worker reactors, read in code (the dispatch of a request to the handler, the multi-worker overload's signature, how connections and h2c streams are assigned to workers, any API that runs a handler off the reactor and posts its answer back);
- wire tests in real child processes, with a handler held by a pipe (M3-045's `held`), so that whether a second request progresses before the first is released is decided by the order of events, not by sleeps or CPU speed: HTTP/1.1 and h2c separately, the h2c client acknowledging the server's SETTINGS; each child reaped within a bound (a child that outlives it is killed and the test fails);
- the same tests against Flare's own `HttpServer` with a Flare-only handler, single-worker and, where it builds, multi-worker (the second only as evidence about Flare, never as a Muntin path);
- for any candidate that would call `App.handle` from more than one thread: an account of every piece of state it reaches (the `App`'s routes and erased handlers, `_Shared`'s counts, `State[S]` values, middleware, the JSON cap's memory bound) and whether Mojo 1.1.0 can make the compiler reject a state type that is unsafe to share.

**Candidates.**
- A, Flare's multi-worker `serve`: a `Copyable` handler sharing the borrowed `App` across worker threads, a worker count on `Server`. Only if the safety account above holds.
- B, separate the reactor from handler execution: the reactor hands each request to other threads and the answer goes back to the reactor that owns the connection. Only if Flare v0.12.0 offers the hand-off and the way back.
- C, keep one reactor per `Server` and recommend several OS processes (each binding its own `Server`), stating what improves and what remains.
- D, decision only: if no safe implementation exists, pin the current blocking with tests and record what Flare or Mojo would need.

**Comparison criteria:** progress of other connections while a handler blocks; progress of other streams of the same h2c connection; CPU use across cores; the ownership safety of `App` and `State` (who may touch them from which thread, and what the compiler checks); compatibility of `Server.bind`/`serve`, M3-044's receive limit and M3-045's stop and one-`serve`-per-process claim; the code added; dependence on Flare internals; testability on Linux x86-64 and macOS arm64.

**Pass conditions** for an implementing candidate (each on the wire, on both CI systems): a test that fails before the change and passes after, for each protocol the change claims to improve; a test that pins what it does not improve; the safety account above with each claim backed by a test, a fixture or the compiler; scratch mutations that turn the new tests red; M3-044's and M3-045's tests and the serving fixtures unchanged and passing. If no candidate meets them, D.

**Read in code** (Flare v0.12.0, the pinned commit):
- Single worker: the loop (`flare/http/_unified_reactor_impl.mojo`, `_run_unified_loop_for_fd`) polls, then advances the idle-timer wheel (`_advance_timer_wheel_unified`), then handles the poll's events one at a time. HTTP/1.1 calls `handler.serve(req^)` inline in `ConnHandle.on_readable` (`flare/http/_reactor/conn_handle.mojo`); h2c calls it inline, once per completed stream, in a loop in `Http2ConnHandle.on_readable` (`flare/http/_h2_conn_handle.mojo`). While a handler runs, the thread accepts, reads, writes and times out nothing. Flare's `docs/concurrency.md`: "flare uses a thread-per-core reactor with **synchronous** handlers … `def serve(req) raises -> Response` runs on a pthread worker and *blocks that worker until it returns*."
- Multi-worker (`serve[H: Handler & Copyable](mut self, var handler: H, num_workers: Int, pin_cores: Bool = True)`, `flare/http/server.mojo`): closes the bound listener and starts a `Scheduler` whose workers each get `handler.copy()` and their own reactor, and, by default, their own `SO_REUSEPORT` listener (`FLARE_REUSEPORT_WORKERS=0`: one shared listener). A connection stays on the worker that accepted it for its whole life (`docs/concurrency.md`: "Connections are owned by one reactor worker for their entire lifetime"), so all streams of an h2c connection go to one worker. Each worker still runs its handler synchronously.
- `HttpServer.drain` closes `self._listener` and then sets the stop flag. On the multi-worker path that listener was already closed by `_serve_multicore`, and the per-worker listeners belong to the `Scheduler`, which `drain` does not reach (`Scheduler.drain` exists, but `HttpServer` never calls it). So M3-045's stop, run on the multi-worker path, would keep accepting new connections for the whole window (read in code, not measured).
- Off-reactor execution: no handler trait completes later. `block_in_pool` runs a function on a new pthread but its caller blocks until `pthread_join` (its docstring: releasing the reactor "would need either Mojo async or a new 'park this connection' reactor state"). The one way to get a completion back into a reactor, `StreamConn.attach_upstream(fd)` with `serve_streaming`, is a different handler trait (`StreamHandler`), HTTP/1.x only and without TLS. `Reactor.wakeup()` exists but nothing calls it.
- Thread safety: Flare's `docs/concurrency.md` says the pinned Mojo has "no compiler-checked notion of state that is safe to share across threads (no `Send` / `Sync` traits)", quoting Modular's forum, and that the standard library's `String`/`List`/`Dict` reference counts are not safe to share. Muntin did not verify either claim; the decision below does not rest on them.

**Measured** (Mojo 1.1.0, Flare v0.12.0, Linux x86-64 container with 4 CPUs (macOS arm64, the pull request's CI runner: every observation in the table identical, resets included; the first macOS run failed four h2c cases because macOS `setsockopt` rejects a receive timeout on a connection the server has reset with `EINVAL`, so the client now sets its timeouts while the connection is open); the retained tests in `adapters/flare/test_server.mojo`, "Head-of-line blocking (M3-046)", three runs each, all alike). Each test holds request A's handler on a pipe (M3-045's `held`, which also writes `a` to the pipe when released), sends a light request whose handler writes `b` to the same pipe, waits `HOLD_PROBE_MS` (1 s) for its answer, releases A, reads every answer, ends the child within a bound (`Server`: SIGTERM, exit 0 required; Flare's server: SIGKILL), and only then reads the pipe to its end. The pipe's order is what the tests assert about progress; it does not depend on timing. `kind` is `Server` with `blocking_app`; Flare's own `HttpServer` serving `_FlareHold` (the same routes with no Muntin code) with its default configuration; and the same with `idle_timeout_ms` 60 s ("patient"), to separate two effects:

| Case | While A is held (1 s) | After A is released | Handler order |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP/1.1, keep-alive connection answered before the hold, request sent during it | not answered | `Server` and Flare: closed with its request unread (reset), no answer; patient: answered | `Server`, Flare `ab` (its handler never ran); patient `abb` |
| HTTP/1.1, new connection opened during the hold | not answered (queued by the system; Flare does not call `accept` while a handler runs, read in code) | answered | as above |
| HTTP/1.1, A's own connection (keep-alive) | — | A answered, then the connection closed; patient: not checked | — |
| h2c, stream 3 on A's connection (SETTINGS acknowledged before the hold) | not answered | A's stream 1 answered, then the connection reset with stream 3 unread; patient: stream 3 answered | `Server`, Flare `a`; patient `ab` |
| h2c, stream 1 on another connection set up before the hold | not answered | that connection reset with its stream unread; patient: answered | `Server`, Flare `a`; patient `ab` |

- **Two effects.** (1) Serial dispatch: no other handler ran before A's returned, on any connection or stream, in every case and every kind. (2) Flare's idle timer, read in code: the loop advances the timer wheel once per iteration, after the poll and before the events, and `TimerWheel.schedule` arms a timer relative to the wheel's last tick (`flare/runtime/timer_wheel.mojo`), which a long handler leaves stale. So every idle timer armed before the handler or during the same iteration (A's own connection after its answer, any connection handled later in that batch) is due within `idle_timeout_ms` (500 ms by default; Muntin does not set it) of that stale tick, and the next iteration's advance fires it before reading the events that arrived meanwhile: the connection is closed although its request has arrived. What decides a drop is a connection's idle time before the handler plus the handler's run time, not the run time alone (a 100 ms handler can drop a connection already idle for 450 ms; read in code, not measured); a connection with a partly received request or awaiting its h2c preface has the same timer. With a hold of 1 s, the tests show the drops: requests on already open keep-alive and h2c connections get no answer, and A's own keep-alive connection is closed right after its answer; only connections still queued by the system are answered afterwards. With the patient configuration every request was answered after A.
- **Cause.** Flare alone behaves exactly as `Server` does in every case, so neither is Muntin's code: it is Flare's single reactor running a synchronous handler, plus its timer order.
- **More workers** (scratch, not retained: the Flare-only handler declared `Copyable`, `serve(..., num_workers=N, pin_cores=False)`, patient configuration, Linux only). With one handler held: of 16 new HTTP/1.1 connections, 7 to 9 were answered during the hold with 2 workers, 11 or 12 with 4 (three runs): the kernel's `SO_REUSEPORT` hash still sends some connections to the held worker, where they wait. Of 8 new h2c connections, 7 and 8 (two runs) completed their SETTINGS and a stream with 4 workers. Stream 3 on the held stream's own connection was not answered during the hold, as with one worker, and was answered after it. More workers improve progress across connections, probabilistically by the hash; they do nothing for streams of one h2c connection.
- **Several processes** (scratch, not retained, Linux only): `Server.bind` once, then two forked processes each calling `server.serve(app)` on the shared listener. With one process's handler held, 16 of 16 new HTTP/1.1 connections were answered during the hold (three runs): the held process does not poll, so the other accepts every connection. Not measured on macOS; not a supported form today (below).

**The safety account for running `App.handle` on several threads (A and B).**
- What `App.handle` reaches: the `App`'s route list and erased handlers (read, not changed, by `handle`), per-request values (the request copy, decoded route values, a JSON tape), `_Shared`'s count (atomic), and the application's `State[S]` values, borrowed with no count change (M3-001).
- `State[S]` is read-only only through `state[]`, and shallowly: "a type `S` with interior mutability … changes under its own rules, and Muntin does not synchronize it" (M3-001). Applications may have such types today (M3-001's spike counted calls through an `ArcPointer[Int]` in `Users.calls`); they are single-threaded because `App.handle` is never called concurrently, which M3-001 and `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` state as the reason they are safe. Running `handle` on several threads could turn those whose interior mutability is not synchronized (atomics or a lock would be safe) into data races, without a compile error or a change to the application's code. Muntin has no way today to require `S` to be safe to share: no marker trait on `State`, and none that Muntin knows the compiler checks. Requiring one would change `State`'s contract (M3-001, M3-004), which is a decision of its own, not this item's. Workers as an opt-in with a documented thread-safety obligation on the application is rejected for the same reason: it would be an unchecked rule in a framework whose point is checked ones.
- Middleware is compile-time functions with no state of their own, but middleware reads what handlers read. The JSON cap bounds memory per parse, "one per `App` today" (M3-008): N workers multiply it.
- The borrowed `App`'s lifetime would hold (Flare's multi-worker `serve` joins its workers before it returns, and `serve` borrows the `App` for that call), but that is the only part of the account that holds.

**Candidates, compared.**

| Candidate | Other connections | Same h2c connection | CPU | `App`/`State` safety | Compatibility | Code, Flare internals | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: Flare's multi-worker `serve`, a `Copyable` borrowed handler, a worker count on `Server` | improves, by the kernel's hash (7 to 12 of 16 measured), not deterministically | no change | N cores | fails the account: concurrent `handle` can make a `State[S]` with unsynchronized interior mutability, which Muntin accepts today, a silent data race; no compile-time check available | breaks M3-045: `drain` leaves the per-worker listeners accepting for the whole window; the `_BorrowedHandler` guard would be removed | small in Muntin; relies on Flare's multi-worker drain, which does not work | rejected |
| B: reactor and handler execution separated | would improve both, if the answer could go back | would improve | N threads | same failure as A (handlers on other threads) | — | Flare v0.12.0 has no deferred response or way back for `Handler` over h1 and h2c; building one is a Muntin reactor/executor, which AGENTS.md rules out without a milestone | rejected: not expressible on Flare v0.12.0 |
| C: one reactor per process; several processes | another process's connections progress (16 of 16 when they share a listener) | no change | one core per process | unchanged: each process's `App` stays on one thread | unchanged | none today; making the shared-listener form supported needs its own stop semantics (each process's `drain` closes only its copy of the listener) | kept as operational guidance, without a new supported form |
| E: the adapter sets a longer `idle_timeout_ms` (no API change; a scratch adapter setting 60 s answered every waiting request of the `Server` cases after the hold) | unchanged: still blocked during a handler; waiting requests are answered after it instead of dropped, up to the new threshold | no change | — | unchanged | changes, for every application, the keep-alive idle close that `docs/DX.md` section 1 documents and M3-045's stop tests time against (500 ms); idle connections hold descriptors and connection slots longer (Flare's `max_connections`), so idle clients cost more | one line in `_server_config`; departs from M3-032's "Flare's defaults for everything else" | rejected for this item: it moves the threshold rather than removing it, and choosing a server-wide idle timeout is backend configuration, which M3-032 leaves to its own decision (revisit condition below) |
| D: decision only; pin the blocking; record what Flare and Mojo would need | — | — | — | unchanged | unchanged | tests only | **chosen**, with C as guidance |

**Selected: D.** `Server` keeps one reactor and calls `App.handle` on one thread. The blocking is now pinned on the wire (`adapters/flare/test_server.mojo`: `Server` over HTTP/1.1 and h2c, and the same cases on Flare alone, default and patient) and documented (`docs/DX.md` section 1, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`). `src/muntin`, the adapter, `Server`'s API, M3-044's limit, M3-045's stop and claim, and the `_BorrowedHandler` guard are unchanged.

- **What applications are told** (`docs/DX.md` section 1): one request's handler holds every other request of the process; a long handler can make Flare's idle timer close open keep-alive and h2c connections that waited meanwhile, with their requests unanswered (reproduced with a 1 s hold; the general rule is read in Flare's code): it can lose requests rather than only delay them. Handlers must therefore be short. Requests that must make progress while one is slow are served by several processes, each with its own `Server`, behind a load balancer (each process binds its own port). That improves progress across processes only: within one process, and for every stream of one h2c connection, it is as above.
- **Why not the shared-listener form as supported now** (a candidate for a later serving-lifecycle item, `docs/SPEC.md`): it was measured once, on Linux, and its stop has different semantics (a process that stops closes only its copy of the listener, so new connections keep being accepted by the others; one stop then refuses nothing on that address). Making it supported is a serving-lifecycle item with its own tests, not part of this decision.

**What Flare would need** (upstream, for A or B to become possible):
- multi-worker `drain` that closes every worker's listener and drains every worker (`Scheduler.drain` reached from `HttpServer.drain`), so M3-045's contract can hold with workers;
- a handler completion that does not hold the reactor, for HTTP/1.1 and h2c: park a connection or stream, run the handler elsewhere, post the response back (Flare's `block_in_pool` names this as a follow-up);
- dispatch of h2c streams that does not run one connection's streams in sequence on one thread, for streams of one connection to progress at all;
- the idle timer not closing a connection whose request has already arrived: advance the wheel's clock after a handler returns (before arming timers) and handle readable events before expiring timers; re-arming on readiness alone would not do, since the timers are armed from the stale tick. That would make a long handler cost delay instead of lost requests even with one worker.

**What Mojo or Muntin would need:** a way for Muntin to require at compile time that a `State` value (and anything else a handler shares) is safe to use from several threads, or an accepted decision that changes `State`'s contract to such a bound. Until then no concurrent `App.handle` can be shown safe.

**By kind (M2-016): not an M2 reopen.** Nothing `App.handle` answers, no API and no diagnostic changes; tests and documentation of the current behavior only.

**Cost.** Throughput and latency under slow handlers stay bounded by one thread per process, and a handler longer than 500 ms drops waiting keep-alive and h2c requests. The new tests take about 14 s of the `Server` suite (each holds a handler for 1 s and stops its child).

**Revisit when:**
- Flare's multi-worker `drain` stops new connections on every worker, or Flare offers a deferred handler completion for HTTP/1.1 and h2c: revisit A or B, still subject to the safety account;
- Mojo gains a compiler-checked notion of thread-safe sharing, or a decision gives `State` a thread-safety bound: revisit the safety account;
- the blocking tests' observations change (a light request answered during the hold, or a waiting keep-alive or h2c request answered after a hold longer than the idle timeout): Flare changed its dispatch or timer order; revisit `docs/DX.md` section 1 and this record;
- `Server` gains backend configuration ([M3-032](#serving-entrypoint-decision-m3-032)): an `idle_timeout_ms` would let an application trade the dropped requests for longer waits; revisit the guidance;
- an application asks for several processes serving one address as a supported form: a serving-lifecycle item (its stop semantics, macOS, tests).

**Next action: explicit deferral.** No production slice follows: the revisit conditions above name what would make a concurrent `Server` decidable.

### Server idle timeout decision (M3-047)

Status: **decision and production** (M3-047, [pull request #85](https://github.com/sano-suguru/muntin/pull/85); `src/muntin` unchanged). It decides whether `Server` should let an application set Flare's `ServerConfig.idle_timeout_ms`, which `Server` leaves at Flare v0.12.0's default (500 ms). Two records name it: [M3-032](#serving-entrypoint-decision-m3-032) ("applications need a backend limit or protocol setting changed (body size, timeouts, TLS): revisit whether `Server` takes a Muntin-owned configuration") and [M3-046](#head-of-line-blocking-decision-m3-046) ("`Server` gains backend configuration: an `idle_timeout_ms` would let an application trade the dropped requests for longer waits"), which declined its candidate E (the adapter setting a longer timeout for everyone) because it would change every application's keep-alive close. The question, candidates, criteria and pass conditions below were written before any measurement; what precedes them was read from the records named above and from Flare v0.12.0's source.

**Why now.** M3-046 pinned that a handler running longer than the idle timeout (counting a connection's idle time before it) makes Flare close open HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and h2c connections whose requests arrived meanwhile, unanswered: with the default, such a handler loses requests rather than only delaying them, and an application has no way to change that short of building Flare's `HttpServer` itself, which M3-032 rejected as API.

**Question.** Should `Server` expose Flare's idle timeout, and if so how: its spelling and where it lives; whether every existing `Server.bind(...)` call and `server.serve(app)` keep building and answering exactly as today, the 500 ms default included; the unit, the valid values and where an invalid one is caught (0, which Flare documents as "disables", a negative value, a value whose arithmetic in Flare could overflow, and the largest value worth accepting); whether one value reaches HTTP/1.1 and h2c alike; what a longer value changes on the wire (requests that waited behind a long handler answered after it, never during it) and what it does not (the blocking itself); what it costs (idle connections, and connections that never send a byte, held longer); how it interacts with M3-045's stop (the grace window, the bound, the keep-alive close during the window); whether two `Server`s keep their own values; and what changes in the accepted set, the overload set, the diagnostics and the runtime, classified against M2-016.

**What it is not.** Other timeouts (`write_timeout_ms`, `read_body_timeout_ms`, `request_timeout_ms`, `handler_timeout_ms`, which Flare does not enforce), keep-alive limits, connection counts, TLS and workers are out of scope; so is any change to the blocking itself (M3-046's deferral stands).

**Candidates.**
- A, a keyword-only argument of `Server.bind`: `Server.bind(host, port, *, ..., idle_timeout_ms=n)`, whose omission keeps the 500 ms default, checked by `bind` before anything is bound and written by the adapter into Flare's configuration.
- B, a typed timeout configuration: a Muntin-owned type (for example `Timeouts(idle_ms=...)`) passed to `bind`, holding this timeout now and others later.
- C, change the default: the adapter sets a longer idle timeout for every `Server`, with no API change (M3-046's candidate E).
- D, decision only: leave the API and the adapter unchanged, and record the blockers and revisit triggers.

**Comparison criteria**, per candidate: the spelling beside `max_body_bytes` and `shutdown_grace_ms`; the public API added; whether every existing call keeps building and answering as today with the same default on both protocols; ownership; how the next setting would be added; the unit, range and zero semantics, and where an invalid value is caught, with what message; whether one value reaches HTTP/1.1 and h2c, and how a partial propagation would be caught; the effect on M3-046's dropped requests and on its pinned default-configuration tests; the cost of idle connections; the interaction with M3-045's stop; whether Flare types reach application code (A1, A2); the code added; accepted set, overload set, diagnostics and runtime by kind (M2-016). The smallest candidate that meets the pass conditions is chosen; a configuration is not chosen merely because it can be built.

**Pass conditions** for an implementing candidate (each with executable evidence in real child processes, each child reaped within a bound):
- with an explicit timeout longer than a 1 s held handler, a request sent during the hold on an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection answered before the hold, stream 3 on the held stream's h2c connection, and stream 1 on another h2c connection set up before the hold are each answered after the release and never during the hold, and no other handler runs before the held one returns (the order pipe); these tests fail before the change;
- with no value given, M3-046's default-configuration tests pass unchanged (the waiting requests dropped), so the default is still 500 ms on both protocols;
- two `Server`s bound in one process with different values keep their own;
- the range's boundaries, zero included, are checked by `bind` with the message the record names, before anything is bound (on a port a child serves, so a raise is not `AddressInUse`), and the accepted ends bind;
- SIGTERM still stops a `Server` bound with a long idle timeout within its own `shutdown_grace_ms` and bound (the window plus 1 s), with an idle keep-alive connection open, exit 0;
- `max_body_bytes`, `shutdown_grace_ms`, the one reactor, the signal claim, `_BorrowedHandler`'s non-`Copyable` guard, the serving fixtures and every existing test are unchanged and pass; `src/muntin` is unchanged and `check_boundaries.sh` passes;
- scratch mutations, each turning a listed test red: the propagation removed (the value never reaching Flare's configuration), the default changed, and the validation broken (each end).

If no candidate meets them, D: the API and the adapter stay unchanged, and the record names the blockers and what would lift them.

**Read in code** (Flare v0.12.0, `8c6e1400`):
- `ServerConfig.idle_timeout_ms: Int`, default 500, documented "Max ms a connection may stay idle before the reactor closes it (default 500), including a connection that has not sent its first byte yet. 0 disables." It is one field: the HTTP/1.1 handle (`flare/http/_reactor/conn_handle.mojo`) and the HTTP/2 handle (`flare/http/_h2_conn_handle.mojo`, whose `on_readable` and `on_writable` take the `ServerConfig`, not `Http2Config`) both re-arm their timer with it after each read and each completed write, and the accept loop arms it for every new connection (`_arm_accept_timer`), so one value reaches both protocols. Unlike M3-044's body limit there is no second field.
- Zero and negative values: `_arm_accept_timer` arms nothing for a value `<= 0`; the per-step re-arm (`_apply_step`, `_apply_step_h2`) cancels the connection's timer for 0 and ignores a negative value (`-1` is the "unchanged" sentinel of `StepResult`). So 0 and any negative value leave every connection without an idle timer. `ServerConfig.check` (compile time, not called by `HttpServer`) asserts only `>= 0`.
- Large values: `TimerWheel.schedule` computes `fire_at = current_tick + UInt64(delay)` (a 512-slot wheel of 1 ms slots, longer delays in an overflow list promoted once per rotation); for any `Int` up to `Int.MAX` that sum stays below 2^64, so nothing overflows; a value that large never fires.
- Which timer applies when: the idle timer while nothing has arrived, between keep-alive requests, after every h2c read or write (a stalled h2c body included: nothing in Flare's HTTP/2 path reads `read_body_timeout_ms`), and while an HTTP/1.1 head is incomplete; while an HTTP/1.1 body is still arriving, `read_body_timeout_ms` (30,000) instead, and while a response is being written, `write_timeout_ms` (5,000). `request_timeout_ms` (60,000 from a request's first byte) is checked only when bytes arrive, so it never closes a connection that has gone silent: the idle timer is the only bound on a connection that never sends a byte or stalls inside its head.
- The stale tick (M3-046): timers are armed relative to the wheel's last advance, which a long handler leaves behind, so a connection is closed after a hold when its idle time before the handler plus the handler's run time exceeds the idle timeout. A longer timeout moves that threshold; it does not remove the serial dispatch or the stale tick.
- M3-045's stop: `drain` keeps the reactor serving open connections for the whole window and the reactor then closes every connection still open (`_drain_remaining_conns_unified`), whatever its timers. The idle timer only closes connections earlier, inside the window.

**Measured** (Mojo 1.1.0, Flare v0.12.0, Linux x86-64; a scratch probe, not retained, served a fixed `200 hello` handler on Flare's own `HttpServer` with `idle_timeout_ms` set, two runs each unless noted; then the retained tests in `adapters/flare/test_server.mojo`, "Idle timeout (M3-047)"):
- **Default and timing.** `ServerConfig().idle_timeout_ms` is 500. With 500, 1,000 and 2,000, an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection after its answer, a connection that never sent a byte, and an h2c connection after the SETTINGS exchange were each closed (EOF) 500 to 505, 1,000 to 1,002 and 2,000 to 2,005 ms later.
- **0, −1 and `Int.MAX`:** each of the three connections stayed open for the probe's whole 3 s: no idle timer, as read in code. Nothing crashed.
- **Partial requests**, with 500 and 2,000: a head without its blank line was closed at the idle timeout (503, 2,002 ms); a complete head declaring 100 bytes with 10 sent stayed open past 3 s with both values (the 30 s body timer).
- **Tiny values:** with 1 ms, of 20 requests each written right after `connect`, 19, 20, 20 and 19 were answered (four runs); with 5 ms, 20 of 20 each time. A timeout shorter than a client's gap can close its connection first.
- **Idle cost** (Linux, `/proc`): 500 connections that never send a byte took the serving process from 6 to 506 file descriptors and its RSS up by about 0.8 to 1.5 MB (1.5 to 3 KB each) in three runs; 1.5 s later the 500 ms server was back at 6 descriptors and the 60 s server still held 506. The memory was not returned to the system after the close in either case. `ServerConfig.max_connections` is 0 (unlimited), so the process's descriptor limit is what bounds them.
- **`Server`, red before the code:** the new tests did not build against the base (`invalid call to 'bind': unexpected keyword argument 'idle_timeout_ms'`); against a scratch adapter that accepted the keyword but did not write it into Flare's configuration (so it served exactly as the base does), all seven failed, and M3-046's three `Server` cases passed (an eighth test, added after the docs were drafted, failed the same way: with 1,000 given, a silent connection, an incomplete HTTP/1.1 head and an idle h2c connection were closed after 500 to 502 ms): the waiting keep-alive request was dropped (`''`, reset), stream 3 and the other h2c connection's stream were dropped (handler order `a`), and under SIGTERM with a 1,500 ms window the idle keep-alive and h2c connections were closed after 499 and 501 ms, by the idle timer.
- **`Server`, with `idle_timeout_ms=60_000`** (green): with a 1 s held handler, nothing was answered during the hold; afterwards the keep-alive request and the new connection were answered (order `abb`), stream 3 on the held stream's connection and the stream on another h2c connection were answered (order `ab`). Under SIGTERM with a 1,500 ms window, new connections were refused after 48 ms, the idle keep-alive and h2c connections were closed 1,636 ms after the signal (the window's end) and the child exited 0 after 1,693 ms. Two `Server`s bound in one process, with 3,000 and with no value, closed an idle keep-alive connection after 3,000 and 500 ms. With 1,000, a silent connection, an incomplete head and an idle h2c connection, each opened and timed on its own, were closed after 1,000 to 1,003 ms, and an HTTP/1.1 request stalled inside its body was still open after about 3,000 ms (three runs, after the review below; an h2c stream stalled inside its body was added after the scoped review and closed at the idle timeout). M3-046's default-configuration cases passed unchanged.

**Candidates, compared.**

| Candidate | Spelling | Public API added | Old calls and default | Values | Both protocols | Effect on M3-046's drops | Cost of idle connections | M3-045's stop | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: a keyword-only argument of `Server.bind` | `Server.bind("0.0.0.0", 8080, idle_timeout_ms=30_000)` | one keyword argument with a default | every call builds and keeps 500 ms on both protocols (M3-046's tests unchanged) | checked by `bind` before anything is bound, with Muntin's message | Flare's one field; tests over HTTP/1.1 and h2c | an application whose handlers can run long turns the drops into waits (measured) | its choice: each idle connection holds a descriptor and 1.5 to 3 KB for the chosen time | unchanged bound; idle connections close at the window's end instead of earlier (measured) | **chosen** |
| B: a typed timeout configuration | `Server.bind(h, p, timeouts=Timeouts(idle_ms=n))` | a public type, its initializer and fields, and an argument | as A if the argument has a default | as A, in the type or at `bind` | as A | as A | as A | as A | rejected: a type for one independent integer; M3-044's rule keeps keyword-only arguments until settings must be built, validated or shared as one value, which nothing here needs (revisit below) |
| C: a longer default | none | none | changes every existing `Server`: keep-alive and silent connections are held longer, M3-046's pinned drops become waits, and M3-045's documented 500 ms close inside the window moves | none for the application | as A | removes the drops up to the new default, for everyone | every application pays for idle connections, including those with short handlers that never needed it | as A | rejected: the right value depends on the application's slowest handler and its clients, which Muntin cannot know; it would also undo the goal of keeping defaults unchanged that M3-044 and M3-045 kept |
| D: decision only | none | none | unchanged | none | none | none: an application can only shorten handlers or run several processes (M3-046), neither of which helps a slow handler's own process | none | unchanged | rejected: A meets every pass condition with one keyword argument, and the hazard it addresses (requests lost, not only delayed) has no other remedy within a process |

**Selected: A. `Server.bind(host: String, port: Int, *, max_body_bytes: Int = 10485760, shutdown_grace_ms: Int = 5000, idle_timeout_ms: Int = 500) raises -> Server`.** The adapter writes the value into Flare's `ServerConfig.idle_timeout_ms` before binding. Contract: `docs/DX.md` section 1.
